lessons.title: The Great Pyramid of Giza
lessons.description: The oldest of the seven wonders, the only one still standing, and how it was actually built.
lessons.contents:
There was once a powerful man, a Pharaoh named Khufu. Khufu had many great dreams, but none so great as his dream of a remarkable tomb. The tomb that he dreamt of would become what we now know as The Great Pyramid of Giza. We begin our module with this ancient wonder for many reasons, but most notably because it is the oldest of the ancient seven wonders, but also because it is the only ancient wonder left standing today.

Once the pyramid was completed, it stood at about 150 meters tall. This meant that for almost 4,000 years, it was the tallest building on earth. Nothing that any society or person built came close to this size up until cathedral spires went up in Europe sometime in the 1300s. The structure itself is crafted out of around 2.3 million blocks of stone. The average weight of those blocks was about the weight of a hippopotamus and the largest of the blocks weighed as much as 10 elephants.

For many years it was assumed by historians that slaves were responsible for the actual building of the pyramids; however, archaeologists digging near Giza found something very different than they expected. They discovered that the workers who built the pyramids had villages where they lived and were celebrated. These workers were given honorable burials and enjoyed things like bakeries and breweries in their day to day life. What we learned was that these workers were paid, fed, and even worked as a team.

Building a great structure like the pyramid must happen in controlled sections. This is because each step of the building process was very important and even the smallest change to this order or process could have resulted in disaster. The first step for the workers would be flattening out the ground and clearing anything, like trees, shrubs, or other structures, so that the pyramids would sit on level ground. This is because a pyramid-like structure built on a slope would slowly tear itself apart with time. After this, stone needed to be mined from quarries and moved to the building site. Once the stone was delivered to the building site, the core of the pyramid was built, piece by piece. Finally, came the casing. The casing used on the pyramid was a smooth layer of limestone, applied like a shell over top of the stone structure. This casing was cut, fitted over the outside of each block, and then polished to be smooth and was known to be bright white and reflective. This made it so the pyramid would glisten in the sun.

You may be wondering how the pyramid could have been white. Every picture you have likely seen of the Great Pyramid of Giza does not reflect that final step. This is because of an earthquake that shook a lot of the limestone casing off sometime in the 1300s CE. When this happened, many people took the stones covered in limestone that fell and used them to build other structures in Cairo nearby. So, when you look at a picture of the pyramid today, what you are really seeing is the inside of the structure, not what it would have looked like thousands of years ago.

lessons.title: The Hanging Gardens of Babylon
lessons.description: A wonder nobody has ever found, and the argument over whether it existed at all.
lessons.contents:
Our next lesson will cover one of the most mysterious of the ancient seven wonders, one that may have never existed at all. This ancient wonder is known as the Hanging Gardens of Babylon. The mystery surrounding this wonder begins around 600 BCE. An ancient king, known as Nebuchadnezzar II, married a woman from a distant land. When she came to Babylon, she discovered that she hated the terrain of flat, brown plains and greatly missed the lush, lively, greenery filled landscape she once called home. The king wanted to provide her comfort in her new home and so he decided to build a great garden that stretched up high into the sky, filled with terraces, trees growing out of the walls, and with water carried through every inch of the great structure to keep everything alive.

This story about Nebuchadnezzar and his wife is a beautiful story, but ultimately a flawed one. The issues arise when we investigate where this story comes from. Every existing description of the story itself and the Hanging Gardens of Babylon was written by Greek and Roman authors hundreds of years later. They were only writing down what they had been told by someone else or what they had read in books. The strangest part is, Babylon's own records never mention a famous garden. Even stranger still, in the early 1900s an excavation team spent years searching through Babylon. They found walls, gates, and streets, but not anything indicating the remains of a grand garden.

Recently, there was a scholar who came up with a brand new theory surrounding these mysterious gardens. Her name is Stephanie Dalley. Stephanie argued that the gardens were real, but that everyone had been looking in the wrong city. It was her belief that the gardens truly resided in the city of Nineveh, which is about 300 miles north of Babylon. In Nineveh, there were carvings boasting a terraced garden with water being lifted up into it. Furthermore, there was an Assyrian king named Sennacherib who is noted as speaking about building exactly those gardens around 700 BCE. Stephanie's idea is that the story drifted from one city to another over the centuries and the credit ended up attached to the wrong king.

This ancient wonder leaves us with many unanswered questions. Where were the Hanging Gardens of Babylon? Did they ever exist at all? Who originated the story of Nebuchadnezzar and his wife? The truth is, nobody has quite settled those questions yet. Sometimes the lack of an answer can be more interesting than knowing the exact details, because it means there is something there to investigate or some problem to solve.

lessons.title: The Lighthouse of Alexandria
lessons.description: A tower built to solve a problem, and what each of its three sections did.
lessons.contents:
Alexandria was one of the most notable cities in ancient history. Picture this: a brand new sprawling city ruled by the Ptolemies, a Greek family who ruled Egypt after Alexander the Great's death, with one serious problem. The Egyptian coast surrounding the city was low, flat, and sandy with no cliffs or hills for a ship's captain to navigate with. This led to many ships running aground in an attempt to locate the harbor. This led the Ptolemies to build a great landmark that could not be missed, even in the most bleak conditions.

The construction of the Lighthouse of Alexandria was started under Ptolemy I and finished by his son around 280 BCE. It was located on a small island called Pharos just off the coast of the city. The lighthouse itself stood at around 100 meters tall and for centuries, the only building on Earth that was taller was the Great Pyramid.

The lighthouse was built with three unique sections stacked one on top of the other, with each section being a different shape. The bottom section was in the shape of a square and was by far the largest of the three. It contained rooms inside for the workers and a long ramp that animals climbed to haul fuel for the light up the tower. The second section above it was an eight-sided, or octagonal, section that carried the tower higher and narrower. At the very top was the final section, which was round on all sides and at its peak burned the fire that made the lighthouse glow.

You may be wondering how just a fire could have shone bright enough through darkness and storms to guide wayward ships. The truth is, the fire on its own would not have been enough to lead the way. In order to magnify the flame's light, a polished metal mirror stood behind it and cast light out over the water. Many ancient writers actually claimed that sailors could see the light from almost 30 miles away and a few even claimed that the mirror itself could set enemy ships ablaze. Now, the claim that this metal mirror was able to cause a ship to catch fire is almost certainly false, but it is a testament to how impressive people found this structure at the time.

The Lighthouse of Alexandria stood for roughly 1,600 years, quite a long life for such a stately building. Unfortunately, it was destroyed by earthquakes over time and finally in 1480 CE, the last of its stone went to building a fort that still stands on the same spot the lighthouse once stood.

lessons.title: The Statue of Zeus at Olympia
lessons.description: A statue so big it nearly hit the ceiling, and what it was actually made of.
lessons.contents:
Every four years, athletes from all across Greece made the long trip to a place called Olympia to compete in the Olympic Games. These games were held in honor of Zeus, who was believed to be the king of all the Greek gods, so it only made sense that Olympia would have a temple built for him. The people of Olympia started building that temple around 470 BCE. Once it was finished though, there was still something missing, and that something was Zeus himself.

The job of creating a statue of Zeus was given to a sculptor named Phidias, who had already made a name for himself in Athens. Sometime around 435 BCE, Phidias completed his statue. It showed Zeus sitting on a throne, and even seated, the statue stood at about 12 meters tall. That is about as tall as a four-story building. The statue was so large that Zeus's head nearly reached the ceiling of the temple, which led an ancient writer named Strabo to joke that if Zeus were to ever stand up, he would take the roof off with him. In his right hand, Zeus held a smaller statue of Nike, the goddess of victory, and in his left he held a scepter with an eagle sitting at the top of it.

You may be wondering what a statue like this was even made of. The truth is, it was not made out of one material at all. On the inside was a wooden frame that worked much like a skeleton does and held the entire statue up. Phidias then covered that frame in thin plates of carved ivory for Zeus's skin and sheets of gold for his robe and sandals. Ivory has a habit of cracking once it dries out, so the workers at the temple would treat the statue with olive oil to keep it protected. Statues made from gold and ivory like this one are called chryselephantine statues, a name that comes from the Greek words for both materials.

For a very long time, the only things we knew about the statue came from what ancient writers had to say about it. This changed in the 1950s when archaeologists digging beside the temple uncovered the workshop that Phidias had used to build the statue. Inside of the workshop were clay molds that had been used to shape the gold. Even more exciting was a small cup that was found with the words "I belong to Phidias" scratched into the bottom of it. This was proof that the workshop really had belonged to the same sculptor that the ancient writers described.

The Statue of Zeus stood for roughly 800 years, but how it was eventually destroyed is still a mystery. Some ancient accounts claim that it was taken to the city of Constantinople and was later lost in a great fire there. Other accounts say that it burned in Olympia along with the temple it was built for. Both of these events supposedly took place sometime in the 400s CE, but since not a single piece of the statue has ever been found, nobody can say for certain which story, if either, is the true one.

lessons.title: The Temple of Artemis at Ephesus
lessons.description: A temple that was built twice, and the man who burned the first one down just so people would remember him.
lessons.contents:
Along the coast of what we now know as the country of Turkey, there once stood a great city called Ephesus. This city was a busy port, and the people who lived there worshipped the Greek goddess Artemis. Because many people in the city were devoted to Artemis, there had been temples to the goddess on this spot for a long time; however, sometime around 550 BCE, a prominent king named Croesus funded the creation of a temple that would be much larger and grander than those that came before it. This new temple was to be built almost entirely out of marble, which at this time was a very rare building material, and even rarer still for a building of this size. The building itself was about 115 meters long, which means it was longer than the Lighthouse of Alexandria was tall! It had more than 100 tall marble columns lining the outside, creating a beautiful frame around the magnificent building.

One day, tragedy struck the temple. In 356 BCE, a man named Herostratus set fire to the temple and it burned to the ground. You may be wondering why someone would burn down such a lovely building intended for worship, and chances are it was not for the reasons you might think. He did not set fire to the temple because he wanted to steal the valuables nestled inside, nor did he burn it down because he had a problem with the worship of the goddess Artemis. He actually said that his reason for burning down the temple was that he wanted his name to be remembered forever, long after he had left this earth. The citizens of Ephesus were rightfully furious and ended up passing a law that stated nobody was allowed to say his name ever again; however, as you may have noticed, here we sit more than 2,000 years later speaking about that very man, so the law did not quite work out the way that they had hoped.

In the aftermath of the temple's destruction, the people of Ephesus decided that they did not want to leave their temple in ashes. They decided that they would rebuild on the same spot where the ruined temple had stood and that this time, they would make the temple even larger than before. The reconstructed temple is the one that ancient writers actually put on their list of the seven wonders of the ancient world. Alexander the Great offered to assist in rebuilding the temple, but the Ephesians refused, as he wanted his name carved into the temple. They felt it would be wrong for one god to build a temple for another, as people at this time saw Alexander the Great as such.

This second grand temple stood for almost 600 years. In 268 CE, the temple was severely damaged during a raid by the Goths. In the centuries that followed, the temple was abandoned and much of its marble was carried away to be used in the construction of other buildings. Over time, it slowly disappeared until nobody even knew where it had once stood. That is, until 1869, when, after six years of searching, a British architect named John Turtle Wood finally found what was left of the temple buried underneath several meters of mud. Today, the only thing left at the site is a single column that has been pieced back together from broken fragments, marking the spot where the great Temple of Artemis once stood.

lessons.title: The Mausoleum at Halicarnassus
lessons.description: A tomb so famous that the name of the man inside it became the word we use for grand tombs today.
lessons.contents:
Have you ever heard the word mausoleum before? This word is central to our lesson, and it is important that we discuss what it means before we dig into the meat of our topic. A mausoleum is an above-ground building or structure intended to house burial chambers, caskets, or remains after someone has passed. This word also has a very interesting origin: it comes from the name of a real person, Mausolus, who was the ruler of a region called Caria, which is located in what is now known as southwestern Turkey. Mausolus ruled Caria from its capital, Halicarnassus, a city along the coast that we now know as Bodrum.

Mausolus died in 353 BCE. His wife, Artemisia, felt very strongly about giving Mausolus a tomb unlike anything else in the world at the time. It is unclear whether plans for the tomb began before or after Mausolus' passing, but it is known that Artemisia took control of building it once he had passed. She secured the best architects and artists she could find to work on the tomb and create something truly magnificent. The architects and artists she enlisted to work on the tomb included four of the most famous Greek sculptors of the time. Each of those sculptors was tasked with decorating one side of the tomb with carvings of battles and scenes from Greek myths. Artemisia never lived to see the finished product these creatives worked on, as she herself passed away only two years after her husband. There are records from a notable Roman writer that state the sculptors actually stayed behind and finished their work anyway because they knew that a tomb as grand as this one would make them famous.

The completed tomb stood at about 45 meters tall and was built in layers, each one stacked on top of the last. The base, located at the very bottom, was made entirely of stone and held the burial chamber itself. Directly above the base was a ring of 36 marble columns. Atop those columns was a roof shaped like a stepped pyramid. At the very peak stood a statue. This statue depicted four horses pulling a chariot. In fact, there were statues all over the building, which made it just as much of a work of art as it was a tomb.

The Mausoleum at Halicarnassus stood for well over 1,000 years before a series of earthquakes destroyed most of it. Throughout the 1400s and early 1500s, a group of knights, known as the Knights of St. John, took the fallen stones from the tomb and used them to build and strengthen their castle. That castle, located in Bodrum, still stands in the city's harbor today. Later, in the 1850s, an archaeologist named Charles Newton dug up the site and found pieces of the old sculptures, some of which can still be seen today at the British Museum in London.

lessons.title: The Colossus of Rhodes
lessons.description: A giant bronze statue paid for by a failed attack, and the famous pose it most likely never had.
lessons.contents:
Around 305 BCE, the island of Rhodes faced serious trouble. A powerful general named Demetrius had surrounded the island's main city with a massive army and some of the largest war machines ever built. The people of Rhodes would not go down without a fight, and they actually managed to hold out against the siege for about a year. In the end, Demetrius gave up and sailed away, leaving much of his equipment behind.

The people of Rhodes developed a plan in the aftermath of this event. Their plan was to sell off all that abandoned equipment and use the money to build a giant statue of Helios, the sun god, as a way of thanking him for protecting their city. They chose a sculptor by the name of Chares of Lindos to work on this statue. It took Chares around 12 years to finish his work on the Colossus of Rhodes, and when the statue was finally completed, around 280 BCE, it stood at about 33 meters tall. This meant it was nearly the same height as the Statue of Liberty from her feet to the top of her head.

To construct this great statue, Chares needed to take great care. He started with a frame on the inside made of iron bars and stone columns, which gave the statue much-needed strength and support. Then, he covered that frame in thin plates of bronze that were shaped to look like the body of the god Helios. Historians are still unsure exactly how the bronze plates were added onto the frame, with one ancient writer suggesting that workers would pile up huge mounds of dirt as the statue grew so that they could continue climbing up to reach the next section.

It is possible that you have seen pictures of the Colossus standing with one foot on each side of the harbor while ships sail underneath it. That famous image is almost certainly incorrect though, as a bronze statue with its legs spread that far apart would not have been able to support its own weight. Building it that way would also have meant closing the harbor for the 12 years it took to build the statue, which is very unlikely to have happened. Today, most historians agree that the Colossus stood with its feet together on a base somewhere near the harbor, but the exact spot where it stood has never been discovered.

Unfortunately, the Colossus only stood for around 54 years. In 226 BCE, a strong earthquake hit Rhodes and snapped the statue at the knees, which sent the rest toppling to the ground. Ptolemy III, the king of Egypt at the time, offered to pay for the rebuilding of the statue, but the people of Rhodes refused based on a warning from an oracle. This meant that the Colossus stayed exactly where it fell for around 800 years, and many people would travel to Rhodes just to get a glimpse of the giant broken pieces of the fallen statue. One writer of that time wrote that very few people could wrap their arms all the way around its thumb, showing just how large the statue truly was. Later writers state that in the 650s CE, Arab forces who took over Rhodes sold off whatever bronze was left for scrap.
